title: NY State Assembly · District 85
area: South and southeastern Bronx, including Hunts Point, Longwood, Soundview, Clason Point and Harding Park.

context.text: Uncontested race. Incumbent Emerita Torres, first elected in 2024, is the only candidate on the November 3 ballot; no Republican or Conservative Party candidate qualified for the general election.

candidates.name: Emerita Torres

summary.text: Emerita Torres is the Democratic and Working Families Party nominee for re-election in NY Assembly District 85, a South Bronx seat she has held since January 2025, and is running unopposed. A lifelong Bronx resident, she spent about a decade as a U.S. State Department diplomat, then worked at The Soufan Center and the Community Service Society before winning the seat in 2024. She sits on the Aging, Banks, Consumer Affairs and Protection, Economic Development, Education and Housing committees.

background.text: A lifelong Bronx resident who, according to her Assembly biography, grew up with parents who relied on public assistance programs and rent-stabilized housing. Her campaign website describes her as being of Puerto Rican heritage.
The first in her family to graduate from college; earned a B.A. in history from New York University and a master's degree in public policy from the Harvard Kennedy School of Government.

Served roughly a decade as a U.S. diplomat with the State Department, with postings including Brazil, Pakistan, Colombia, Washington, D.C. and the United Nations, working on labor rights, climate change, peacekeeping and protecting women's rights in conflict. Her campaign website says she received three Meritorious Honor Awards and a Superior Honor Award.

Served as Director of Policy Research and Programs at The Soufan Center, working on disinformation, terrorism and the rise of authoritarianism; her Assembly biography says her advocacy led to the sanctioning of the first white supremacist group in U.S. history.

Served as Vice President of Policy, Research and Advocacy at the Community Service Society, where she worked on expanding New York's half-price MetroCard program, tenants' rights, homeownership and rental-assistance reform, and co-led the National True Cost of Living Coalition's efforts.

Has served on the boards of the Bronx River Arts Center and the Women's Housing and Economic Development Corporation (WHEDco); her campaign website also lists her as a two-term State Committee member for the 85th Assembly District and a Term Member of the Council on Foreign Relations.

Won the Assembly District 85 seat in the November 5, 2024 general election with 78.9% of the vote, defeating Republican Kelly Atkinson and Conservative Gary Lutz, after the previous member, Kenny Burgos, resigned over the summer; she took office January 1, 2025.

Her Assembly biography says she organized deliveries of personal protective equipment and food to Bronx families during the COVID-19 pandemic and has mentored Bronx middle and high school students; it says she lives in the Soundview section of the Bronx with her partner and two children.

priorities.text: Affordability, fairness and opportunity for Bronx families, and directing investments back to the district.
Keeping housing affordable and protecting longtime residents and working families from displacement.
Universal childcare, which she has led on in the state legislature as essential infrastructure for working families.
Protecting immigrant New Yorkers from harm and discrimination.

positions.summary: Says she led the fight for universal childcare in the state legislature, calling it essential infrastructure for working families and economic stability.

Describes herself as an outspoken advocate for immigrant New Yorkers and says she co-sponsored the New York for All Act, which would limit state and local involvement in federal immigration enforcement.

record.text: Secured over $8 million in new investments for the district for local services, infrastructure and community priorities in her first year in office.
Directed $7 million toward keeping housing affordable in the district.

Allocated $1 million in discretionary funding across community development, youth programs, gun-violence prevention, arts education, climate resilience, healthcare affordability and food-insecurity efforts.
Passed what her campaign describes as a first-in-the-nation surveillance-pricing disclosure law requiring corporations to disclose when they use personal data to set prices.
Invested in forming a merchants' association along the Westchester Avenue corridor to support small businesses and local jobs.
Worked to stop a vehicular expansion of the Cross Bronx Expressway, citing pollution and traffic concerns.
